policy_title: Itemized Bill Review for Inpatient Routine Services
related_policies: Itemized Bill, Outpatient Claim Itemized Bill Review

extracted_content.title: Overview
extracted_content.content: Facility billing guidelines for the UB-04 claim form, also known as the CMS-1450, and the 837 institutional electronic equivalent require providers to bill revenue codes to describe services rendered. Revenue codes are categorical and do not describe exact items, supplies and services provided during an inpatient admission. Humana may request an itemized bill for an inpatient facility claim to verify that billed revenue codes represent charges for appropriately billed items, supplies and services. Routine items, supplies and services already included in the primary inpatient room and board charge are not separately billable.

extracted_content.title: Medicare Advantage Payment Policy
extracted_content.content: In addition to the policy, claims payments are subject to other plan requirements for the processing and payment of claims, including, but not limited to, requirements of medical necessity and reasonableness and applicable referral or authorization requirements. Humana sometimes reviews an itemized bill for an inpatient admission to determine whether supplies, items and services specified on the itemized bill are separately billable. To separately bill for items, supplies and services rendered during an inpatient hospital encounter, the provider must consistently follow its customary charging practices for all Medicare and non-Medicare patients, for all payers and health plans. The following supplies, items and services are typically not separately billable and, therefore, not separately payable from the general room and board charge or primary service charge. Please note that the examples given do not represent an exhaustive list.

extracted_content.title: Medicare Advantage Payment Policy
extracted_content.content: Any supplies, items and services that, under customary charging practices, are included in charges for a specific service or in charges for the delivery of services in a specific location. Examples of included supplies and items are bandages and inpatient admission kits. Examples of included services are IV flushing, dressing changes, equipment monitoring and routine nursing care and assessments.

extracted_content.title: Medicare Advantage Payment Policy
extracted_content.content: All items and supplies that may be purchased over the counter, such as personal care items, ice packs, alcohol wipes and cotton balls.

extracted_content.title: Medicare Advantage Payment Policy
extracted_content.content: All reusable items, supplies and equipment that are provided to all patients on a routine basis during an inpatient admission; this applies to all types of inpatient admissions, including an admission to a specific treatment area, such as a NICU or CCU, and applies to the admission of a patient who is receiving the same types of service as a patient in a specific treatment area. Examples of reusable items, supplies and equipment are cardiac monitors and durable medical equipment (DME) items used while inpatient.

reimbursement_guidelines.title: Reimbursement Guidelines
reimbursement_guidelines.content:
In addition to the policy, claims payments are subject to other plan requirements for the processing and payment of claims, including, but not limited to, requirements of medical necessity and reasonableness and applicable referral or authorization requirements. Humana sometimes reviews an itemized bill for an inpatient admission to determine whether supplies, items and services specified on the itemized bill are separately billable. To separately bill for items, supplies and services rendered during an inpatient hospital encounter, the provider must consistently follow its customary charging practices for all Medicare and non-Medicare patients, for all payers and health plans. The following supplies, items and services are typically not separately billable and, therefore, not separately payable from the general room and board charge or primary service charge. Please note that the examples given do not represent an exhaustive list.

Any supplies, items and services that, under customary charging practices, are included in charges for a specific service or in charges for the delivery of services in a specific location. Examples of included supplies and items are bandages and inpatient admission kits. Examples of included services are IV flushing, dressing changes, equipment monitoring and routine nursing care and assessments.

All items and supplies that may be purchased over the counter, such as personal care items, ice packs, alcohol wipes and cotton balls.

All reusable items, supplies and equipment that are provided to all patients on a routine basis during an inpatient admission; this applies to all types of inpatient admissions, including an admission to a specific treatment area, such as a NICU or CCU, and applies to the admission of a patient who is receiving the same types of service as a patient in a specific treatment area. Examples of reusable items, supplies and equipment are cardiac monitors and durable medical equipment (DME) items used while inpatient.

In addition to the policy, claims payments are subject to other plan requirements for the processing and payment of claims, including, but not limited to, requirements of medical necessity and reasonableness and applicable referral or authorization requirements. Humana Medicaid plans review inpatient itemized bills with routine services according to applicable state Medicaid agency requirements.

Customary charging practices: A provider's common or established practice for classifying a particular item or service that is consistently followed for all patients and does not result in an inequitable apportionment of cost to the Medicare Program.

Room and board charge: Inpatient routine services in an inpatient facility generally are those services included by the provider in a daily service charge, which is sometimes referred to as the room and board charge. The room and board charge includes the room, dietary and nursing services, minor medical and surgical supplies, medical social services, psychiatric social services and the use of certain equipment and facilities for which a separate charge is not payable.

Routine: Inpatient routine services in an inpatient facility generally are those services included by the provider in a daily service charge, sometimes referred to as the room and board charge. Some examples of routine services include the room, dietary and nursing services, minor medical and surgical supplies, medical social services, psychiatric social services and the use of certain equipment and facilities for which a separate charge is generally not payable.
